phrases.translation: ˹This is˺ a discharge from all obligations, by Allah and His Messenger, to the polytheists you ˹believers˺ have entered into treaties with
phrases.explanation: The chapter opens without the usual opening formula and begins with a public announcement. Allah and His Messenger declare themselves released from treaty obligations toward those Arab polytheist groups who had broken their agreements with the believers. A discharge of this kind gave open notice that protection under those treaties was ending, rather than allowing a surprise attack.

phrases.translation: “You ˹polytheists˺ may travel freely through the land for four months,
phrases.explanation: The announcement still grants a clear respite. For four months the treaty breaking groups could move through the land in safety, settle their affairs, and consider their position. The period functions as a warning interval between the public notice and any enforcement. Mercy and urgency stand together here, because time is given but the time is limited.

phrases.translation: but know that you will have no escape from Allah, and that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers.”
phrases.explanation: No respite can place anyone beyond the reach of Allah. Travel, alliances, and distance might delay human action, yet they cannot frustrate the judgment of God. The promised disgrace means public failure for those who persisted in hostility after fair warning. The verse therefore removes false confidence while the door created by the four months remains open.

phrases.translation: A declaration from Allah and His Messenger ˹is made˺ to all people on the day of the greater pilgrimage that Allah and His Messenger are free of the polytheists.
phrases.explanation: The declaration was proclaimed openly on the day of the greater pilgrimage, when large numbers were gathered and news could reach every tribe. Publicity mattered because treaties, pilgrimage, and safe passage affected the whole region. Allah and His Messenger are declared free of the polytheists who had violated their commitments, so no one could later claim ignorance of the change.

phrases.translation: So if you ˹pagans˺ repent, it will be better for you.
phrases.explanation: Repentance is presented as the better path still available during the warning period. To repent here means abandoning idolatry and hostility and accepting the new order established around worship of Allah alone. The benefit belongs to the repentant themselves, since turning back would bring safety in this world and hope of forgiveness in the next.

phrases.translation: But if you turn away, then know that you will have no escape from Allah.
phrases.explanation: Turning away after a clear public warning carries a different warning. Such people cannot escape Allah by leaving a territory, hiding among allies, or relying on numbers. The words cut off the assumption that rejection has no consequence. They also frame the coming conflict as judgment on persistent treaty breaking rather than a sudden change of mood.

phrases.translation: And give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to the disbelievers of a painful punishment
phrases.explanation: The phrase good news is used with biting irony. What awaits unrepentant disbelievers is painful punishment, so the announcement to them is the opposite of glad tidings. A similar ironic address appears elsewhere in the Quran when warning replaces welcome. The closing line keeps the proclamation solemn, because ease is promised to repentance and hardship to defiance.

phrases.translation: As for the polytheists who have honoured every term of their treaty with you and have not supported an enemy against you,
phrases.explanation: An exception is stated before any wider ruling is applied. Some polytheist groups had kept every term of their agreement and had not helped an enemy against the believers. Their conduct separates them from the treaty breakers addressed in the opening verses. Faithfulness to an agreement is therefore judged group by group and act by act.

phrases.translation: honour your treaty with them until the end of its term.
phrases.explanation: The believers must honour such treaties until the agreed term expires. The end of other agreements gives no excuse to break faith with people who kept theirs. This limitation is central to the passage, since it shows that the discharge was not a blanket licence. A promise remains binding while the other side remains true to it.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah loves those who are mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: The closing words give the reason for restraint. Mindfulness of Allah includes fearing Him in public dealings, especially when power has shifted in your favour. Keeping a treaty with a weaker partner becomes an act of piety, not only a political calculation. Allah loves those whose conscience governs their conduct when breaking faith would be easy.

phrases.translation: But once the Sacred Months have passed, kill the polytheists ˹who violated their treaties˺ wherever you find them,
phrases.explanation: This verse concerns the hostile treaty breakers after their announced respite ended. The sacred months and the four months of safe travel formed a protected interval in which fighting was withheld. Once that interval passed, the believers were commanded to confront those who remained at war with them. Groups that kept their treaties remained protected under the previous verse.

phrases.translation: capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them on every way.
phrases.explanation: The commands to capture, besiege, and lie in wait describe the military pressure of that historical campaign. The aim was to end the power of groups that had repeatedly violated agreements and threatened the community and pilgrimage routes. Every way points to blocking movement and escape routes. Read with its exceptions, the verse addresses a defined conflict in Arabia.

phrases.translation: But if they repent, perform prayers, and pay alms-tax, then set them free. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: Even here the door of repentance remains open. If former opponents turn back, establish prayer, and pay the alms tax, they are to be released and left safe. Prayer and alms are named because they are visible signs of entering the believing community. The verse ends with forgiveness and mercy, placing reconciliation above continued fighting.

phrases.translation: And if anyone from the polytheists asks for your protection ˹O Prophet˺,
phrases.explanation: Protection could be requested even by an individual polytheist during this tense period. The Prophet is told to grant safe conduct to such a person rather than treat every outsider as a combatant. A request for protection created a duty of safety under the customs of the time. The verse turns a possible enemy encounter into an opportunity for hearing.

phrases.translation: grant it to them so they may hear the Word of Allah,
phrases.explanation: The purpose of the protection is that the visitor may hear the word of Allah. Safe conduct is given for listening and reflection, not as a trap and not under pressure of immediate danger. The person hears the message in security and can judge it after direct exposure. Invitation therefore continues alongside the conflict with treaty breaking groups.

phrases.translation: then escort them to a place of safety, for they are a people who have no knowledge
phrases.explanation: After hearing, the protected person must be escorted to a place of safety, even if he does not accept the message. The reason given is lack of knowledge, since people who have not yet heard clearly should not be treated as deliberate rejecters. This safeguard limits the fighting commands and shows that safe passage was a binding trust.

phrases.translation: How can such polytheists have a treaty with Allah and His Messenger,
phrases.explanation: The question asks how a lasting treaty could stand with groups whose record showed repeated betrayal. A treaty with Allah and His Messenger requires trust, restraint, and respect for sacred commitments. Where those foundations had already collapsed, treating the document as healthy would ignore experience. The verse begins by challenging the assumption that every signed agreement still deserves confidence.

phrases.translation: except those you have made a treaty with at the Sacred Mosque? So, as long as they are true to you, be true to them.
phrases.explanation: One group is excepted, namely those who made their treaty at the Sacred Mosque and remained true to it. As long as they stay straight with the believers, the believers must stay straight with them. Reciprocity is the rule, so loyalty is answered with loyalty. This exception again shows that conduct, not identity alone, decided how a group was treated.

phrases.translation: Indeed Allah loves those who are mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: The verse closes as verse four closed, with love for the mindful. Keeping faith with treaty partners who keep faith is part of fearing Allah. The repetition fixes the principle in the reader mind before the passage returns to the treachery of others. Strength does not cancel conscience, and victory does not cancel a promise.

phrases.translation: How ˹can they have a treaty˺? If they were to have the upper hand over you,
phrases.explanation: The rhetorical question is repeated, and the reason follows. If these groups gained the upper hand, their past conduct showed what would happen to agreements. Power would remove the restraint that weakness had imposed on them. The believers are asked to judge the treaty by the character already displayed, not by pleasant words spoken under pressure.

phrases.translation: they would have no respect for kinship or treaty.
phrases.explanation: Kinship and treaty were the two great restraints recognised in Arabian society. Family ties should have softened conflict, and sworn agreements should have bound conduct even between rivals. To respect neither meant that no normal safeguard could be trusted. The accusation is severe because it describes people released from both natural loyalty and public obligation.

phrases.translation: They only flatter you with their tongues, but their hearts are in denial, and most of them are rebellious
phrases.explanation: Their speech and their hearts pull in different directions. Flattering words buy time and safety, while inward denial waits for a better opportunity. Most of them are called rebellious because the pattern was deliberate rather than accidental. The verse teaches the believers to read conduct over time, since a tongue can promise what the heart refuses.

phrases.translation: They chose a fleeting gain over Allah’s revelations, hindering ˹others˺ from His Way.
phrases.explanation: A fleeting gain means the small worldly advantage gained by breaking faith, pleasing allies, or keeping old privileges. They traded the revelations of Allah for that brief benefit and also blocked others from His way. The exchange is presented as a poor bargain, because what was sold was lasting guidance and what was bought soon passes away.

phrases.translation: Evil indeed is what they have done
phrases.explanation: The judgment on the bargain is brief and complete. Their deed is called evil because it joined personal betrayal with public harm, turning others away from the path they themselves rejected. The short sentence works like a verdict after the description. It leaves no room to describe treaty breaking for profit as cleverness or harmless politics.

phrases.translation: They do not honour the bonds of kinship or treaties with the believers.
phrases.explanation: The charge is restated in its plainest form. With believing relatives and treaty partners alike, they honoured neither bond. Where kinship should have created mercy and agreements should have created restraint, both were set aside when hostility became useful. Repetition of the charge shows that this unreliability, rather than a single incident, sits behind the opening discharge.

phrases.translation: It is they who are the transgressors
phrases.explanation: Such people are named transgressors because they cross recognised limits. Transgression here is not only private sin but public aggression against the ties that make shared life possible. The label explains why trust had collapsed and why firm measures followed in that setting. It also warns readers that breaking bonds for advantage carries a moral name.

phrases.translation: But if they repent, perform prayer, and pay alms-tax, then they are your brothers in faith.
phrases.explanation: The same door opened in verse five is opened again. Repentance joined with prayer and alms tax changes former opponents into brothers in faith. Brotherhood is a strong word, because it cancels the old enmity and creates duties of care and protection. Past hostility is not held over people who genuinely enter the community of belief.

phrases.translation: This is how We make the revelations clear for people of knowledge
phrases.explanation: The closing sentence explains why these distinctions are spelled out so carefully. Allah makes the signs clear for people who know, meaning people willing to learn the differences between treaty keepers, treaty breakers, seekers of protection, and new believers. Knowledge here is practical discernment. The passage can only be applied justly when its categories are kept apart.

phrases.translation: But if they break their oaths after making a pledge and attack your faith,
phrases.explanation: A new case is described, namely people who swear a pledge and then break it while also attacking the faith itself. The problem is no longer a lapsed agreement but renewed aggression after a fresh commitment. Mockery or assault on religion joined with oath breaking shows that words of peace were being used as cover for hostility.

phrases.translation: then fight the champions of disbelief—who never honour their oaths—so perhaps they will desist
phrases.explanation: The response targets the leaders or champions of disbelief, those who organised the betrayal and whose oaths carried no weight. Fighting them is given a limited stated purpose, that they may desist. The aim named in the verse is to stop the aggression and oath breaking. Even in conflict language, the end in view is cessation rather than endless revenge.

phrases.translation: Will you not fight those who have broken their oaths, conspired to expel the Messenger ˹from Mecca˺, and attacked you first?
phrases.explanation: The believers are urged not to hesitate when the other side has broken oaths, plotted to expel the Messenger from Mecca, and begun the aggression. Each clause recalls a history that made the conflict defensive in its origin. Memory is used to steady courage, because forgetting who started the wrong can make necessary firmness look like cruelty.

phrases.translation: Do you fear them? Allah is more deserving of your fear, if you are ˹true˺ believers
phrases.explanation: The question about fear reorders their loyalties. Human opponents may look strong, yet Allah deserves fear above every created power. Fear of Allah here means refusing to disobey Him through cowardice or compromise. The final condition ties courage to faith itself, suggesting that trust in Allah becomes visible when obedience is costly and danger is real.

phrases.translation: ˹So˺ fight them and Allah will punish them at your hands,
phrases.explanation: The command to fight is joined to outcomes that belong to Allah. Punishment at the hands of the believers means that human action becomes the means, while judgment remains divine. This framing limits pride, since victory is not credited to numbers or skill alone. It also presents the campaign as an answer to sustained wrongdoing rather than personal vengeance.

phrases.translation: put them to shame, help you overcome them, and soothe the hearts of the believers—
phrases.explanation: Shame for the aggressors, help for the believers, and healing for wounded hearts are promised together. Many believers carried grief from persecution, expulsion, and broken agreements, so relief is described in emotional as well as military terms. Healing hearts suggests that justice can close a long period of helpless anger. The verse then flows into the next.

phrases.translation: removing rage from their hearts. And Allah pardons whoever He wills. For Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The healing promised includes removing rage from hearts that had suffered wrong without redress. Yet the passage immediately returns to pardon, because Allah forgives whoever He wills among former enemies who turn back. Knowledge and wisdom close the section, reminding readers that Allah knows each case exactly. Firmness, relief, and mercy are held together without confusion.

phrases.translation: Do you ˹believers˺ think that you will be left without Allah proving who among you ˹truly˺ struggles ˹in His cause˺ and never takes trusted allies other than Allah, His Messenger, or the believers?
phrases.explanation: Believers should not expect their faith to remain untested. Trials make visible who truly struggles for Allah and who keeps secret loyalties toward His opponents. The trusted allies named at the end mark the boundary, since taking confidants from hostile camps while claiming belief divides the heart. Testing therefore reveals in public what was hidden in private.

phrases.translation: And Allah is All-Aware of what you do
phrases.explanation: The closing words ground the test in divine knowledge. Allah already knows every deed, so the proving described in the verse is for people to see and be judged by what they do. Awareness of Allah covers outward marching and inward alliance alike. No one can perform loyalty before others while hiding betrayal from the One who sees all.

phrases.translation: It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while they openly profess disbelief.
phrases.explanation: Caring for the mosques of Allah includes building, visiting, worshipping, and holding honoured offices around them. The verse denies that role to polytheists who openly witness against themselves by disbelief, since service at a house of worship cannot be separated from the worship itself. Outward maintenance without faith is treated as an empty claim to sacred honour.

phrases.translation: Their deeds are void, and they will be in the Fire forever
phrases.explanation: Because their service rests on disbelief, their deeds are declared void and their end is the Fire. The judgment looks beyond respected public roles to the foundation under them. In the setting of Mecca, old custodians took pride in serving pilgrims while rejecting the message. The verse says that prestige in sacred service cannot replace belief itself.

phrases.translation: The mosques of Allah should only be maintained by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day,
phrases.explanation: The true maintainers of mosques are described by faith before activity. Belief in Allah and the Last Day gives the building its purpose, since a mosque exists for worship and remembrance rather than tribal prestige. Physical care and regular presence both belong to this maintaining. The verse shifts honour from inherited office toward conviction expressed through devotion.

phrases.translation: establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and fear none but Allah.
phrases.explanation: Prayer, alms tax, and fearing none but Allah complete the picture. Such people worship, give, and refuse to let human pressure govern their religion. Fear of others often empties public religion into display, so singling out fear of Allah protects sincerity. A mosque is most alive when the people who uphold it also live by these marks.

phrases.translation: It is right to hope that they will be among the ˹truly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: The ending speaks with hope rather than arrogant certainty. It is right to hope that such people are among the guided, a form of words often read as strong assurance when spoken by Allah. Still, the phrasing teaches humility, since guidance is received as a gift. Service, prayer, and generosity point toward guidance without becoming grounds for pride.

phrases.translation: Do you ˹pagans˺ consider providing the pilgrims with water and maintaining the Sacred Mosque as equal to believing in Allah and the Last Day and struggling in the cause of Allah?
phrases.explanation: Giving water to pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque were honoured Meccan services, and some people measured religious worth by them. The verse asks whether those services, when joined with disbelief, can equal faith, belief in the Last Day, and striving for Allah. The question exposes a confusion between useful public work and the foundation that gives work meaning.

phrases.translation: They are not equal in Allah’s sight. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people
phrases.explanation: The answer is direct. They are not equal in the sight of Allah, because service without belief lacks the root that makes deeds accepted. Wrongdoing people are not guided while they persist in placing prestige above truth. The verse does not deny that water helps pilgrims. It denies that such service can stand in place of faith.

phrases.translation: Those who have believed, emigrated, and strived in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank in the sight of Allah. It is they who will triumph
phrases.explanation: Belief, emigration, and striving with wealth and life are joined as one profile of high rank. Emigration meant leaving home and protection for the sake of faith, while striving put money and personal safety at risk. Together they show a belief that cost something real. Allah ranks such people above comfortable claims, and names them the true triumphant.

phrases.translation: Their Lord gives them good news of His mercy, pleasure, and Gardens with everlasting bliss
phrases.explanation: The reward is announced as good news from their Lord, combining mercy, divine pleasure, and Gardens of lasting bliss. Pleasure of Allah is placed beside Paradise itself, and elsewhere it is described as greater than every other gift. Everlasting bliss means the joy does not spoil, fade, or end in separation. The verse answers costly sacrifice with permanent honour.

phrases.translation: to stay there for ever and ever. Surely with Allah is a great reward
phrases.explanation: The stay in the Gardens is forever, with the repetition underlining that no removal or death follows. Worldly striving involved leaving homes, yet the final home cannot be taken away. The great reward with Allah also corrects human scales, since people may honour visible service while Allah honours sacrificial faith. Permanence is the opposite of every loss they endured.

phrases.translation: O believers! Do not take your parents and siblings as trusted allies if they choose disbelief over belief.
phrases.explanation: Family loyalty is honoured in Islam, yet it finds a limit when parents or siblings choose disbelief and opposition over belief. Taking them as trusted allies here means giving them the loyalty and support that belong against the believers, not simply showing ordinary kindness. The verse guards the community at a time when family ties could become channels of betrayal.

phrases.translation: And whoever of you does so, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: Whoever crosses that limit is named among the wrongdoers, because a lesser loyalty has been placed in the seat of the highest one. Wrongdoing is often putting a thing in the wrong place, and that description fits here. The warning sounds severe because family pressure is powerful. Faith must govern affection, rather than affection quietly governing faith.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If your parents and children and siblings and spouses and extended family and the wealth you have acquired and the trade you fear will decline and the homes you cherish—
phrases.explanation: The list gathers everything that can hold a person back. Parents, children, siblings, spouses, wider family, accumulated wealth, threatened trade, and loved homes each pull on the heart in a different way. Together they describe a complete settled life. The verse names them one by one so that no reader can pretend the warning concerns only the attachments of others.

phrases.translation: ˹if all these˺ are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and struggling in His Way,
phrases.explanation: The test is comparative love. None of these things is condemned by itself, yet they become a problem when they are more beloved than Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His way. Love is proved at the point of conflict, when obeying costs comfort or profit. The verse asks which claim wins when both cannot be served together.

phrases.translation: then wait until Allah brings about His Will.
phrases.explanation: Those who choose their attachments are told to wait for Allah to bring His decision, a warning that history will not wait for their comfort. The command to wait carries threat rather than permission, since delay in obedience already reveals the heart. Events would soon separate the committed from the hesitant. Neutral ground disappears when a direct call has been refused.

phrases.translation: Allah does not guide the rebellious people.”
phrases.explanation: The refusal to guide rebellious people closes the verse with moral clarity. Guidance is not forced on hearts that knowingly prefer wealth and home to Allah. Rebellion here grows from love misplaced rather than from lack of information. The verse therefore examines affection, not only action, and it leaves the reader to ask what truly sits first.

phrases.translation: Indeed Allah has given you ˹believers˺ victory on many battlefields, even at the Battle of Ḥunain when you took pride in your great numbers,
phrases.explanation: Past victories are recalled before the warning hidden inside one of them. At Hunayn the believers were numerous after the conquest of Mecca, and confidence in their size crept into their hearts. Remembering many battlefields establishes that help had always come from Allah. The example then shows how quickly gratitude can turn into pride when numbers look impressive.

phrases.translation: but they proved of no advantage to you.
phrases.explanation: The great numbers proved of no advantage when the enemy ambush struck and ranks broke. A larger army can still panic, lose formation, and flee, especially when confidence rests on counting heads. The verse separates resources from reliance, because means help only when hearts stay firm. Hunayn became a lasting lesson that victory is never owned by the victors.

phrases.translation: The earth, despite its vastness, seemed to close in on you, then you turned back in retreat
phrases.explanation: The image of the wide earth closing in describes the feeling of a rout. Every direction seemed blocked, and the believers turned back in retreat through the valley. Such language captures shame and confusion rather than geography alone. The moment is preserved without flattery, so later readers learn that even a believing community can be humbled by self reliance.

phrases.translation: Then Allah sent down His reassurance upon His Messenger and the believers,
phrases.explanation: Reassurance from Allah steadied the Messenger and the believers after the first shock at Hunayn. This calm, often called serenity, restored courage so the scattered fighters could regroup around the Prophet. The turning point is credited to God rather than to a sudden improvement in numbers. Hearts settled first, and only then could the battle change its course.

phrases.translation: and sent down forces you could not see, and punished those who disbelieved.
phrases.explanation: Unseen forces are mentioned alongside the punishment of the disbelievers, pointing to angelic help beyond human sight. The believers saw the result without seeing every means behind it. Defeat for the opposing force is therefore read as judgment as well as military outcome. The verse teaches that the decisive factors in a crisis may not be visible.

phrases.translation: Such was the reward of the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The brief summary names the outcome as the reward of the disbelievers. Their ambush and hostility ended in the opposite of what they intended, while the believers were corrected and then aided. Reward in this context means fitting return rather than gift. Hunayn thus carries two lessons together, humiliation for arrogance on one side and for aggression on the other.

phrases.translation: Then afterwards Allah will turn in grace to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: After battle and judgment, the passage returns to grace. Allah turns in mercy to whoever He wills among those who fought, fled, or opposed, because repentance can follow even a public failure. Many from the opposing side later entered Islam, and believers who broke ranks were restored. Forgiving and Merciful close the account so that correction does not end in despair.

phrases.translation: O believers! Indeed, the polytheists are ˹spiritually˺ impure, so they should not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year. If you fear poverty,
phrases.explanation: The polytheists are called spiritually impure, a judgment on idol worship rather than a comment on ordinary cleanliness. After that year they were no longer to approach the Sacred Mosque for pilgrimage in the old manner, since the sanctuary was being cleared for worship of Allah alone. The change ended mixed rituals around the Kaaba and completed the opening proclamation.

phrases.translation: Allah will enrich you out of His bounty, if He wills. Surely, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: Loss of pilgrimage visitors raised an economic fear, because trade around Mecca depended heavily on seasonal crowds. Allah answers that provision comes from His bounty and can arrive through new means if He wills. Knowledge and wisdom close the verse, assuring believers that obedience which looks costly is not forgotten. Trust replaces anxiety about income lost through faithfulness.

phrases.translation: Fight those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day,
phrases.explanation: This command addresses a specific political and military setting involving groups from the People of the Scripture who opposed the new order. The descriptions explain why peaceful coexistence had broken down in the view of the verse, since rejection joined with refusal of the public law brought by the Messenger. It belongs to the late Medinan struggles rather than private relations.

phrases.translation: nor comply with what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, nor embrace the religion of truth from among those who were given the Scripture,
phrases.explanation: The phrase religion of truth presents Islam claim to final guidance, while those given the Scripture are Jews and Christians in the surrounding regions. The verse assumes organised communities with their own leadership and armed power, not isolated individuals met in daily life. Reading it in that setting keeps the command tied to public conflict and settlement between polities.

phrases.translation: until they pay the tax, willingly submitting, fully humbled
phrases.explanation: The tax named here is the jizya, a payment under which such communities kept their religion and received protection while accepting the governing order. Fully humbled describes political submission to that settlement after conflict, in the language of the age. Payment ended fighting without requiring conversion. The arrangement differed from the treaty discharge aimed at Arab idol worship around Mecca.

phrases.translation: The Jews say, “Ezra is the son of Allah,” while the Christians say, “The Messiah is the son of Allah.”
phrases.explanation: The verse quotes statements attributed to Jewish and Christian speakers of that era, naming Ezra and the Messiah as son of Allah. Early commentators explained the Ezra statement as the words of a particular group rather than a universal Jewish doctrine. The concern of the verse is theological, since calling any human the son of God conflicts with divine unity.

phrases.translation: Such are their baseless assertions, only parroting the words of earlier disbelievers.
phrases.explanation: Such claims are described as assertions repeated from earlier disbelievers who also gave Allah offspring or partners. Parroting suggests inherited language accepted without proof. In Quranic argument, repetition across generations does not make a claim true. The verse therefore challenges both the content of the saying and the habit of receiving sacred claims without examining them against revelation.

phrases.translation: May Allah condemn them! How can they be deluded ˹from the truth˺
phrases.explanation: The condemnation and the question about delusion express astonishment at turning from clear unity to inherited error. Deluded carries the sense of being diverted from a road that had been visible. The emphasis falls on belief about Allah, since sonship language is treated as a grave distortion. The verse argues theology, and it should not be flattened into a comment about every individual.

phrases.translation: They have taken their rabbis and monks as well as the Messiah,
phrases.explanation: Taking rabbis and monks as lords is explained in early reports as obeying them when they made lawful or unlawful what Allah had decided otherwise. The Messiah is included because worship and obedience due to God were directed toward him. Lordship here therefore concerns authority over religion, not only bowing before a statue or an altar.

phrases.translation: son of Mary, as lords besides Allah, even though they were commanded to worship none but One God.
phrases.explanation: The charge is sharpened by the command they already had, namely to worship One God alone. Their own scriptures called them to unity, so divided lordship cannot be excused as ignorance of the ideal. When human religious leaders are treated as final lawgivers beside Allah, obedience itself becomes a form of association. The verse protects worship by protecting authority.

phrases.translation: There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. Glorified is He above what they associate ˹with Him˺
phrases.explanation: The declaration returns to pure unity. No god worthy of worship exists except Allah, and He is glorified far above partners placed beside Him. Such closing words answer both sonship claims and clerical lordship with one principle. Honouring teachers and honouring Jesus as a prophet must stop short of giving either the place that belongs only to God.

phrases.translation: They wish to extinguish Allah’s light with their mouths, but Allah will only allow His light to be perfected,
phrases.explanation: Blowing at light with mouths pictures the weakness of attempts to end guidance through mockery, denial, and argument. A lamp may be troubled by breath for a moment, yet the image makes the effort look small beside its object. Allah promises instead to complete His light, meaning His religion and proof would reach their intended clarity.

phrases.translation: even to the dismay of the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The completion happens even to the dismay of disbelievers, so their dislike does not control the outcome. History in the passage moves by divine purpose rather than by the permission of opponents. For believers facing ridicule, the verse replaces panic with patience. Opposition can delay comfort and raise noise, yet it cannot decide whether guidance will endure.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who has sent His Messenger with ˹true˺ guidance and the religion of truth,
phrases.explanation: The Messenger is sent with guidance and the religion of truth, joining direction for life with a claim about reality. Guidance shows the road, while truth names the destination and the standard by which other claims are judged. The verse grounds confidence in the sender rather than in the early size or strength of the believing community.

phrases.translation: making it prevail over all others, even to the dismay of the polytheists
phrases.explanation: Prevailing over other religions was understood by early commentators in terms of proof, public establishment, or both, unfolding across time. The dismay of the polytheists repeats the pattern of the previous verse, where dislike cannot veto divine purpose. For the first audience, surrounded by older powers, the promise reversed appearances. Weak beginnings are not evidence of a weak end.

phrases.translation: O believers! Indeed, many rabbis and monks consume people’s wealth wrongfully and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah.
phrases.explanation: Many religious leaders are accused of consuming wealth wrongfully, through bribes, gifts for distorted judgments, or control of offerings. The same influence that took money also hindered people from the way of Allah, because truth became less welcome when it threatened income. The verse addresses believers as a warning, since religious office in any community can be turned into business.

phrases.translation: Give good news of a painful torment to those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in Allah’s cause
phrases.explanation: The warning widens from corrupt leaders to hoarders of gold and silver who refuse to spend in the cause of Allah. Good news is again ironic, because what follows is painful torment. Hoarding here means withholding the rights due on wealth, especially obligatory charity, while treasure sits unused. Money kept from its duties becomes evidence against its keeper.

phrases.translation: The Day ˹will come˺ when their treasure will be heated up in the Fire of Hell,
phrases.explanation: The treasure itself becomes the instrument of punishment on the coming Day. Gold and silver once guarded for comfort are heated in the Fire, reversing their imagined role as protection. The image is deliberate, since what a person trusted to secure the future becomes the means of pain. Judgment gives hoarded wealth a voice it never had in life.

phrases.translation: and their foreheads, sides, and backs branded with it.
phrases.explanation: Foreheads, sides, and backs cover the body from front to back, suggesting a branding that cannot be escaped by turning away. Early explanations pictured plates of treasure pressed against the skin, with each part marked as another was turned toward it. The detail makes disgrace public and complete. Honour sought through accumulation ends as exposure through the same metals.

phrases.translation: ˹It will be said to them,˺ “This is the treasure you hoarded for yourselves. Now taste what you hoarded!”
phrases.explanation: The spoken sentence removes any doubt about the cause. This is the very treasure stored for themselves while rights went unpaid and needs went unmet. Taste what you hoarded turns possession into experience, since they must now feel what they once enjoyed counting. The verse teaches that wealth is a trust, and unused abundance can become a stored punishment.

phrases.translation: Indeed, the number of months ordained by Allah is twelve—in Allah’s Record since the day He created the heavens and the earth—of which four are sacred.
phrases.explanation: Twelve months are fixed in the record of Allah from creation, with four of them sacred. Those four are Rajab and the three surrounding pilgrimage, namely Dhu al Qada, Dhu al Hijja, and Muharram. Sacredness limited fighting so travel and worship could occur in greater safety. The calendar is presented as a divine order rather than a human arrangement.

phrases.translation: That is the Right Way. So do not wrong one another during these months.
phrases.explanation: Calling this the right way gives the calendar moral weight. Wronging one another during sacred months is especially condemned because the protection of those months was meant to restrain violence. Some early readings stressed wronging yourselves through sin in honoured time. Either way, sacred time should produce restraint, and violating it shows contempt for the limits Allah set.

phrases.translation: And together fight the polytheists as they fight against you together.
phrases.explanation: The command to fight together answers a collective threat from the polytheists in that setting, while still sitting beside the rules on sacred months. Unity is stressed because fragmented responses invited attack during vulnerable seasons. The verse joins calendar law to public defence, showing that sacred restraints exist inside real politics. Order requires both reverence and collective responsibility.

phrases.translation: And know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: Knowing that Allah is with the mindful ties obedience to divine support. Withness here means help, protection, and approval for those who respect His limits. The believers could keep sacred months without fearing that restraint left them abandoned. The closing line turns calendar rules into trust, because honouring them places a community under care rather than weakness.

phrases.translation: Reallocating the sanctity of ˹these˺ months is an increase in disbelief, by which the disbelievers are led ˹far˺ astray.
phrases.explanation: Reallocating sanctity refers to the pre Islamic practice of postponing a sacred month, often called nasi. Leaders would declare fighting lawful in a month Allah had made sacred and move the sanctity to another month. The Quran calls this an increase in disbelief because human preference was placed above a divine boundary while keeping a religious appearance.

phrases.translation: They adjust the sanctity one year and uphold it in another,
phrases.explanation: Adjusting one year and upholding another shows that the practice followed convenience. When war or trade made the sacred limit awkward, the calendar was edited. When no pressure existed, the original order could be praised as tradition. Inconsistency exposes the motive, since reverence that appears only when easy is management of religion rather than submission to it.

phrases.translation: only to maintain the number of months sanctified by Allah, violating the very months Allah has made sacred.
phrases.explanation: They kept the number four while violating the actual months Allah sanctified. Counting correctly gave the appearance of obedience, yet the named months themselves were profaned. The verse attacks formal compliance that empties a command of content. A limit can be broken by moving it while boasting that the total still matches, which is obedience in arithmetic only.

phrases.translation: Their evil deeds have been made appealing to them. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people
phrases.explanation: Evil deeds made appealing describes how custom can decorate disobedience until it feels normal and even wise. Once a community praises its own editing of sacred limits, correction sounds like disruption. Allah does not guide people who persist in such disbelief because they refuse the guidance offered. The verse warns against calling a rearranged boundary by the name of faithfulness.

phrases.translation: O believers! What is the matter with you that when you are asked to march forth in the cause of Allah,
phrases.explanation: The call to march forth refers to the Tabuk expedition, a long journey north in intense heat during harvest season. Some believers felt heavy and clung to land, crops, and shade when asked to move. The question what is the matter with you rebukes that heaviness. A command had arrived, yet comfort made obedience feel physically difficult to begin.

phrases.translation: you cling firmly to ˹your˺ land? Do you prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter?
phrases.explanation: Clinging to land becomes a picture of preferring this world over the Hereafter. Farms, homes, and rest were real goods, yet they had started to outrank the call of Allah. The verse asks whether satisfaction with the nearer life explains the delay. When present comfort becomes the measure, a distant reward begins to look unreal and easy to postpone.

phrases.translation: The enjoyment of this worldly life is insignificant compared to that of the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The comparison is settled by scale. Enjoyment in this world is small when placed beside the Hereafter, not because worldly life is worthless but because it ends. Shade during one harvest cannot compare with lasting reward or loss. The verse corrects the eyes before correcting the feet, since people march more readily when the journey is weighed properly.

phrases.translation: If you do not march forth, He will afflict you with a painful torment and replace you with other people.
phrases.explanation: If the believers refuse the call, Allah can afflict them and replace them with other people who will obey. Replacement removes the flattering thought that religion depends on any one generation or group. A community may lose the honour of a task it declines, while the task itself continues. The warning turns hesitation into a question of being set aside.

phrases.translation: You are not harming Him in the least. And Allah is Most Capable of everything
phrases.explanation: No disobedience harms Allah in the least, since His power and kingdom need no human army. Harm falls back on the people who miss reward, invite discipline, and surrender their place. Most Capable of everything closes every escape from that logic. The verse therefore strips bargaining power from reluctance, because Allah gains nothing by their marching and loses nothing by refusal.

phrases.translation: ˹It does not matter˺ if you ˹believers˺ do not support him,
phrases.explanation: Support for the Prophet is first described as something Allah does not depend on. If the believers hold back, the mission is not left helpless, because earlier history already proved where real support comes from. The sentence prepares a memory from the weakest moment of the migration. Present hesitation is answered by a past rescue that no army arranged.

phrases.translation: for Allah did in fact support him when the disbelievers drove him out ˹of Mecca˺ and he was only one of two.
phrases.explanation: When pursuers drove the Prophet from Mecca, he travelled as one of only two, with Abu Bakr beside him. No tribe, treasury, or battle line protected the pair during the escape. Yet that flight became the founding journey of the community in Medina. The verse uses small numbers deliberately, since two hidden men outlasted the power that expelled them.

phrases.translation: While they both were in the cave, he reassured his companion, “Do not worry; Allah is certainly with us.”
phrases.explanation: In the cave, with searchers close enough to cause fear, the Prophet told his companion not to grieve because Allah was with them. The words do not deny danger. They place companionship with Allah above the visible threat outside the cave entrance. This sentence has long been read as a model of calm trust when escape routes look closed.

phrases.translation: So Allah sent down His serenity upon the Prophet, supported him with forces you ˹believers˺ did not see,
phrases.explanation: Serenity descended and unseen forces supported him, just as at Hunayn the decisive help was not fully visible. The pursuers missed what stood almost before them, and the journey continued. Divine help here works through concealment and steadiness rather than public battle. The verse widens the idea of victory to include being protected when no strength is available.

phrases.translation: and made the word of the disbelievers lowest, while the Word of Allah is supreme. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The final contrast makes the word of the disbelievers lowest and the word of Allah supreme. Their plan aimed to end the message at its source, yet the migration gave it a city and a future. Almighty and All Wise explain both the power and the timing of the rescue. What looked like defeat became the doorway to establishment.

phrases.translation: ˹O believers!˺ March forth whether it is easy or difficult for you,
phrases.explanation: The command covers easy and difficult conditions alike, often explained as light or heavy, young or old, rich or poor, eager or burdened. For Tabuk, heat and distance made the second description real for many. No one could wait for a convenient season before the duty counted. Obedience is defined here by response under strain rather than enthusiasm under comfort.

phrases.translation: and strive with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah.
phrases.explanation: Striving with wealth and lives joins funding the effort with personally taking part. Money supplied mounts, food, and equipment, while lives were risked on the road and in possible battle. The pairing prevents a division where some pay without commitment and others risk without support. A community effort needs both forms of sacrifice held together under one intention.

phrases.translation: That is best for you, if only you knew
phrases.explanation: That is best for you returns the benefit to the believers themselves. Allah does not profit from their wealth or danger, yet they gain reward, discipline, and protection for their community. If only you knew points to limited sight, because hardship hides long term good. The verse asks readers to trust a valuation larger than immediate discomfort.

phrases.translation: Had the gain been within reach and the journey shorter, they would have followed you, but the distance seemed too long for them.
phrases.explanation: The excuse makers are exposed by a simple test. Easy gain and a short journey would have attracted them, which shows that interest rather than inability governed the refusal. Tabuk offered distance, heat, and uncertain spoils, so enthusiasm vanished. The verse distinguishes followers of the message from followers of convenience by changing only the cost and watching the response.

phrases.translation: And they will swear by Allah, “Had we been able, we would have certainly joined you.”
phrases.explanation: Their future oath is quoted before it is spoken. By Allah they would claim they would have joined if able, using a sacred name to protect a false excuse. Conditional loyalty sounds reasonable until the earlier test is remembered. Ability in their mouths often meant comfort, profit, and safety combined, which is a different measure from actual capacity.

phrases.translation: They are ruining themselves. And Allah knows that they are surely lying
phrases.explanation: Ruining themselves means the lie damages its speaker more than its hearers. Allah knows the oath is false, so reputation management before people cannot change the record. The sentence closes the gap between public excuse and private motive. A person may escape a journey through words, yet the same words become part of the judgment.

phrases.translation: May Allah pardon you ˹O Prophet˺! Why did you give them permission ˹to stay behind˺ before those who told the truth were distinguished from those who were lying
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is addressed with pardon before reproach, a gentle opening that softens the correction. He had granted some excuse makers permission to remain behind, and the verse asks why this happened before truthful people were separated from liars. Delaying permission would have exposed who intended to stay anyway. Mercy in leadership is praised, yet discernment also protects the community.

phrases.translation: Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask for exemption from striving with their wealth and their lives.
phrases.explanation: True believers in Allah and the Last Day are described by reluctance to seek exemption from costly striving. The point is not that every circumstance ignores illness or real inability, which later verses address. Rather, faith that expects a future judgment does not treat sacrifice as an interruption to life. Eagerness to contribute becomes a sign that belief has settled deeply.

phrases.translation: And Allah has perfect knowledge of those who are mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: Perfect knowledge of the mindful closes the description with a reminder that Allah sees the heart behind each request. Two similar requests can come from opposite motives, one from fear of Allah and one from avoidance. Human leaders judge by evidence, yet final evaluation belongs to God. Mindfulness is therefore measured inwardly as well as by visible participation.

phrases.translation: No one would ask for exemption except those who have no faith in Allah or the Last Day,
phrases.explanation: The pattern is reversed for those without faith in Allah or the Last Day. Exemption seeking becomes their mark because a weakened belief in future accountability makes present cost look decisive. The verse does not read minds at random. It connects repeated avoidance with the convictions that would produce it, especially when excuses gather around every demanding call.

phrases.translation: and whose hearts are in doubt, so they are torn by their doubts
phrases.explanation: Hearts in doubt are torn because uncertainty pulls a person between fear of people and fear of consequences. Doubt does not always speak as open denial. Sometimes it speaks as delay, questions, and waiting to see which side wins. The inner to and fro explains the outer instability, since a heart without anchor keeps changing its public position.

phrases.translation: Had they ˹really˺ intended to march forth, they would have made preparations for it.
phrases.explanation: Real intention normally leaves evidence in preparation. A person planning a hard journey gathers a mount, provisions, and equipment, or at least begins arranging them. Their complete lack of readiness betrayed the excuse before the army moved. The verse teaches a simple reading of sincerity, namely that claims about the future should match present actions taken toward it.

phrases.translation: But Allah disliked that they should go, so He let them lag behind,
phrases.explanation: Allah disliked their going because their presence would have carried harm into the expedition. Being held back is therefore described as both their choice and a divine response to it. Repeated reluctance can harden into inability, where the door once avoided becomes closed from the other side. Their lagging protected the believers even while it exposed them.

phrases.translation: and it was said ˹to them˺, “Stay with those ˹helpless˺ who remain behind.”
phrases.explanation: The words stay with those who remain behind place able bodied excuse makers among women, children, the sick, and others with genuine reasons. The company itself is the rebuke, since they chose the position of the helpless while possessing strength. What they wanted as comfort is given to them as a label. Remaining behind becomes both location and identity.

phrases.translation: Had they gone forth with you ˹believers˺, they would have been nothing but trouble for you,
phrases.explanation: Their absence is then described as a benefit rather than a loss. Had they marched, they would only have increased disorder through complaints, rumours, and wavering at hard moments. An army on a long desert journey depends on morale as much as supplies. The verse corrects any regret over smaller numbers by asking what kind of presence those numbers would add.

phrases.translation: and would have scrambled around, seeking to spread discord in your midst.
phrases.explanation: Scrambling around pictures restless movement through the ranks, carrying talk from group to group and seeking cracks where discord could grow. Fitna here means internal division and doubt during a trial. Such work rarely announces itself as betrayal. It often sounds like caution, inside knowledge, or concern, which makes its spread through a tired company especially dangerous.

phrases.translation: And some of you would have eagerly listened to them.
phrases.explanation: Some believers would have eagerly listened, whether from kinship, past friendship, or simple anxiety on the road. The danger lies in an audience as much as in speakers, because discouraging talk needs ears that pass it on. The verse makes the community examine its own openness to rumour. Protecting unity requires judging reports rather than collecting every alarming voice.

phrases.translation: And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: Perfect knowledge of the wrongdoers closes the matter beyond outward appearances. People may hide under shared language, family ties, or public worship, yet Allah knows the pattern of harm exactly. This knowledge also comforts the believers who marched with fewer companions. What looked like loss of manpower was, in divine assessment, removal of a hidden liability.

phrases.translation: They had already sought to spread discord before and devised every ˹possible˺ plot against you ˹O Prophet˺,
phrases.explanation: Their record did not begin at Tabuk. Earlier plots and attempts to spread discord included stirring old tribal tensions and weakening resolve at sensitive moments. Turning matters upside down against the Prophet suggests trying every angle, public and private, to reverse his position. The verse asks readers to judge excuses against a history rather than as isolated incidents.

phrases.translation: until the truth came and Allah’s Will prevailed—much to their dismay
phrases.explanation: Truth arrived and the command of Allah prevailed despite their dislike. Victories, public order in Medina, and growing acceptance of the message kept disappointing their hopes. Dismay becomes a repeated mark in this chapter because each failure exposes what they wished in secret. The verse turns past frustration into evidence, since sincere allies rejoice when the cause succeeds.

phrases.translation: There are some of them who say, “Exempt me and do not expose me to temptation.” They have already fallen into temptation.
phrases.explanation: One excuse claimed a wish to avoid temptation, often explained through a man who feared he would be tested during the expedition and asked to stay home. The verse answers that refusing the call was itself the temptation into which they had fallen. Pious language can hide disobedience when avoidance is dressed as self protection. The real trial exposed rather than created the heart.

phrases.translation: And Hell will surely engulf the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: Hell engulfing the disbelievers answers their search for safety. They stayed behind to avoid risk, yet the end described surrounds them from every side. The image contrasts a limited worldly danger with inescapable judgment. It also warns against measuring safety only by the next few weeks, since escaping a duty may move a person toward a greater loss.

phrases.translation: If a blessing befalls you ˹O Prophet˺, they grieve, but if a disaster befalls you,
phrases.explanation: Their reaction to events reveals their allegiance. Good fortune for the Prophet grieves them, while disaster gives relief rather than sorrow. People who belong to a community normally share its joys and pains, so reversed emotions expose a hidden separation. The verse reads feelings as evidence, because reactions at unexpected news often say what careful speeches try to conceal.

phrases.translation: they say, “We took our precaution in advance,” and turn away, rejoicing
phrases.explanation: We took our precaution becomes their boast when trouble arrives, as if absence were wisdom rather than avoidance. They turn away rejoicing, pleased that their choice looks vindicated. Such joy at the suffering of supposed companions completes the portrait begun by their excuses. The verse also teaches believers not to measure faithfulness by who can explain events cleverly afterward.

phrases.translation: Say, “Nothing will ever befall us except what Allah has destined for us.
phrases.explanation: The commanded reply places every outcome inside what Allah has written for His servants. Victory, injury, survival, and death do not arrive from the schemes of excuse makers or enemies acting independently. Belief in decree removes both despair and superstition, because events keep their causes yet none escapes divine knowledge. Calm speech becomes an answer to taunting.

phrases.translation: He is our Protector.” So in Allah let the believers put their trust
phrases.explanation: Allah is named Protector, so destiny is not presented as a cold force. The One who decrees also guards, helps, and knows the interests of His servants. Trust therefore means taking lawful means while resting the heart on Him rather than on numbers or forecasts. The final command gathers believers into that trust as a shared discipline.

phrases.translation: Say, “Are you awaiting anything to befall us except one of the two best things: ˹victory or martyrdom˺?
phrases.explanation: The two best things awaiting believers are victory or martyrdom, so the expected outcomes are framed as gain either way. Worldly success brings protection for the community, while death in obedience brings reward rather than simple loss. This outlook removes the enemy power to define every battlefield death as defeat. Hope changes what waiting for news feels like.

phrases.translation: But We are awaiting Allah to afflict you with torment either from Him or at our hands.
phrases.explanation: The other side waits under a different expectation, namely torment from Allah directly or through defeat at the hands of believers. The verse does not grant them a third picture in which hostility ends in honour. Two communities watch the same future with opposite fears. What each side awaits reveals the moral meaning each gives to the conflict.

phrases.translation: So keep waiting! We too are waiting with you.”
phrases.explanation: Keep waiting sounds defiant, yet it also refuses frantic bargaining. Time will disclose which expectation was truthful, and both sides are left facing that disclosure. We too are waiting turns patience into confidence rather than passivity. The believers continue their duty while outcomes ripen, and the excuse makers are left with anticipation instead of excuses.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “˹Whether you˺ donate willingly or unwillingly, it will never be accepted from you, for you have been a rebellious people.”
phrases.explanation: Donations from rebellious people are rejected whether given willingly or under pressure, because the giver relationship with Allah is broken. Money spent for reputation, protection, or social cover may still feed a project outwardly, yet it earns no acceptance as worship. The verse separates the physical transfer of wealth from its spiritual value. Rebellion turns generosity into performance.

phrases.translation: And what prevented their donations from being accepted is that they have lost faith in Allah and His Messenger,
phrases.explanation: The first barrier to acceptance is loss of faith in Allah and His Messenger. Charity in the Quran grows from belief and hope of reward, so giving while inwardly rejecting the message lacks its root. Public generosity can imitate devotion for a while, especially when leaders are watching. The verse looks beneath the gift to the conviction that should have carried it.

phrases.translation: they never come to prayer except half-heartedly, and they never donate except resentfully
phrases.explanation: Lazy prayer and resentful giving show the same inner state in two duties. They attend worship because absence would be noticed, and they donate because refusal would be exposed. Half hearted movement through sacred acts suggests a body present while desire remains elsewhere. Together the signs describe religion carried as social costume rather than love of Allah.

phrases.translation: So let neither their wealth nor children impress you ˹O Prophet˺.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told not to admire their wealth or many children as evidence of divine favour. Large households and property impressed people in that society and could make hypocrisy look successful. Outward increase therefore needs careful reading, since blessing and test can arrive in the same shape. The verse retrains the eye away from size and display.

phrases.translation: Allah only intends to torment them through these things in this worldly life, then their souls will depart while they are disbelievers
phrases.explanation: Those same possessions become a source of torment through anxiety, protection, disputes, loss, and eventual separation by death. What they gather occupies the heart while faith remains absent, so increase deepens attachment rather than gratitude. Souls depart while they are disbelievers, which is the real disaster behind worldly success. Wealth without belief leaves its owner with more to lose.

phrases.translation: They swear by Allah that they are part of you, but they are not.
phrases.explanation: They swear membership in the believing community, using oaths to claim a shared identity. The verse denies the claim at its root, because belonging means loyalty, truthfulness, and shared purpose rather than verbal registration. An oath can assert what conduct has already contradicted. This sharp denial teaches the believers to value tested commitment over repeated declarations made under pressure.

phrases.translation: They only say so out of fear
phrases.explanation: Fear explains the performance. They claim closeness when the believers are strong and distance themselves when danger approaches, always watching which side offers safety. A people of fear in this sense are governed by self protection rather than conviction. Their speech changes with the balance of power, which is why their oaths tell less than their pattern.

phrases.translation: If only they could find a refuge, or a cave, or any hiding-place, they would rush headlong towards it
phrases.explanation: Refuge, cave, and hiding place form a rising picture of panic. If any hole in the earth offered escape from duty and exposure, they would rush toward it headlong like an animal bolting from control. The image is almost comic, yet its point is sad, because people who claim faith are imagined craving disappearance. Fear has replaced purpose as their compass.

phrases.translation: There are some of them who are critical of your distribution of alms ˹O Prophet˺.
phrases.explanation: Criticism of alms distribution exposes another motive behind public religion. Some objected when charity passed them by, treating the Prophet’s decision as unfair because it did not serve their appetite. Distribution of public funds easily attracts complaint when entitlement replaces need as the measure. The verse begins a short lesson that ends with Allah Himself naming the rightful categories.

phrases.translation: If they are given some of it they are pleased, but if not they are enraged
phrases.explanation: Pleasure when given and rage when denied reduce loyalty to payment. The same people can praise fairness while receiving and condemn it while empty handed, which shows that principle was never driving the judgment. Their anger also reveals why donations earlier lacked acceptance. Charity in their world moves in one direction, toward themselves, and stops becoming worship.

phrases.translation: If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them and said, “Allah is sufficient for us!
phrases.explanation: Contentment with what Allah and His Messenger gave would have protected them from resentment. The imagined words Allah is sufficient for us begin by resting need on God rather than on a particular distribution. Sufficiency does not deny poverty or desire. It refuses to let a single decision decide whether Allah is trusted as provider and judge.

phrases.translation: Allah will grant us out of His bounty, and so will His Messenger.
phrases.explanation: Hope then looks forward to future bounty from Allah and through His Messenger administration of lawful gains. A closed door today does not mean provision has ended for the community or the person. This sentence would have replaced complaint with patience while keeping desire honest. It teaches that asking Allah for more can coexist with accepting what He has allotted now.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ we turn with hope.”
phrases.explanation: The closing turn makes hope directional. To Allah alone we turn means desire and expectation gather around Him rather than around officials, luck, or public pressure. Such words would have healed the anger described in the previous verse. The passage contrasts two inner postures toward the same distribution, namely resentment that accuses and longing that trusts.

phrases.translation: Alms-tax is only for the poor and the needy, for those employed to administer it,
phrases.explanation: The alms tax is limited to named classes, beginning with the poor and the needy, whose exact distinction was discussed by early scholars while both point to real want. Administrators are included because collecting and distributing public charity is work that may be paid from it. This opening turns distribution from favour into law, answering complaints with fixed rights.

phrases.translation: for those whose hearts are attracted ˹to the faith˺, for ˹freeing˺ slaves,
phrases.explanation: Hearts attracted to the faith form a category aimed at reconciliation, whether strengthening new believers or softening influential opponents toward peaceful relations. Freeing slaves places liberation inside obligatory charity, so wealth gathered for Allah directly loosens bondage. These two classes show that alms serve social healing as well as hunger. The fund builds safety, belonging, and freedom together.

phrases.translation: for those in debt, for Allah’s cause, and for ˹needy˺ travellers.
phrases.explanation: People in debt are relieved before debt crushes families or pushes them toward wrongdoing. The cause of Allah supports communal needs connected with defence and public good in its classical reading, while stranded travellers receive enough to return home. Together the categories map vulnerability in a whole society. Charity is therefore organised by need and purpose rather than influence.

phrases.translation: ˹This is˺ an obligation from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The list is declared an obligation from Allah, which removes it from the discretion of donors and rulers alike. No complainer can redirect funds by anger, and no distributor can treat them as personal generosity. All Knowing and All Wise close the ruling because the categories rest on knowledge of human need. Justice in charity begins with respecting appointed shares.

phrases.translation: And there are others who hurt the Prophet by saying, “He listens to anyone.”
phrases.explanation: Calling the Prophet one who listens to anyone was a sneer at his willingness to hear excuses and reports. The Arabic image behind the translation is an ear, suggesting someone supposedly ready to believe every speaker. The insult turns patience into gullibility. Behind it stands resentment that private talk kept reaching public light through revelation and observation.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “He listens to what is best for you.
phrases.explanation: The answer reclaims the insult by adding direction. He listens to what is best for them, meaning his hearing serves correction and mercy rather than careless acceptance. A leader may hear a claim without surrendering judgment to it. The verse distinguishes receiving people kindly from being fooled by them, a balance the excuse makers themselves had experienced.

phrases.translation: He believes in Allah, has faith in the believers, and is a mercy for those who believe among you.”
phrases.explanation: He believes in Allah, trusts the believers, and becomes mercy for those who truly believe. Faith in Allah governs what he accepts, while confidence in sincere believers protects community trust. For hypocrites, the same listening becomes exposure rather than comfort. Mercy is therefore selective in effect, since the same Prophet who shelters the sincere also uncovers manipulation.

phrases.translation: Those who hurt Allah’s Messenger will suffer a painful punishment
phrases.explanation: Hurting the Messenger through slander and mockery carries painful punishment. Speech is treated seriously because public contempt weakens trust in guidance and emboldens hidden opposition. The warning also protects the dignity of the message, not only personal feelings. In this chapter, words repeatedly reveal hearts, and harmful words aimed at the Prophet expose settled hostility.

phrases.translation: They swear by Allah to you ˹believers˺ in order to please you,
phrases.explanation: Oaths are again used as social repair, aimed at pleasing believers whose trust has been damaged. Swearing by Allah while seeking only human approval empties the oath of its proper direction. The verse notices the audience they care about, since energy goes into managing neighbours and companions. Image maintenance replaces repentance when applause matters more than truth.

phrases.translation: while it is the pleasure of Allah and His Messenger they should seek, if they are ˹true˺ believers
phrases.explanation: The pleasure that should be sought belongs to Allah and His Messenger. True believers would repair wrongdoing by turning back to the ones actually offended by disobedience. Human approval may follow, yet it cannot be the target. The closing condition tests their claim gently, because seeking divine pleasure is one of the clearest differences between faith and performance.

phrases.translation: Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger will be in the Fire of Hell forever? That is the ultimate disgrace
phrases.explanation: Opposition to Allah and His Messenger is pictured as placing oneself against a boundary that cannot be moved. The result named is lasting punishment in the Fire, described as ultimate disgrace rather than merely pain. Disgrace adds public humiliation to suffering, answering people who cared intensely about reputation. The short verse stops the flow of excuses with a final destination.

phrases.translation: The hypocrites fear that a sûrah should be revealed about them, exposing what is in their hearts.
phrases.explanation: Fear of a revealing surah shows a troubled conscience at work. The hypocrites worry that revelation will announce what private meetings and jokes have hidden. Their fear proves awareness that the inner life does not match the public claim. In a chapter often called the exposer, this dread becomes part of the exposure because innocence rarely fears description.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Keep mocking! Allah will definitely bring to light what you fear.”
phrases.explanation: Keep mocking is a threat in the form of permission. They may continue for a little while, yet Allah will bring out exactly what they fear losing control of. Divine disclosure works through revelation, events, slips of speech, and final judgment. The verse removes the last comfort of secrecy, since hidden contempt is already known to the One judge.

phrases.translation: If you question them, they will certainly say, “We were only talking idly and joking around.”
phrases.explanation: When questioned, they reduce the incident to idle talk and joking. Reports connect the exchange with mocking words spoken during the Tabuk journey about the Prophet and the believers. Calling something a joke is presented as an attempt to shrink its meaning after witnesses reacted. The excuse asks hearers to judge by claimed intention while ignoring the object chosen.

phrases.translation: Say, “Was it Allah, His revelations, and His Messenger that you ridiculed?”
phrases.explanation: The reply names that object directly. Allah, His signs, and His Messenger are not light material for entertainment in the moral world of the verse. A joke can reveal contempt precisely because the speaker felt safe enough to lower guard. The question forces them to face the target rather than hide behind the format of humour.

phrases.translation: Make no excuses! You have lost faith after your belief.
phrases.explanation: Make no excuses ends the negotiation. Their words are judged as loss of faith after a profession of belief, because mockery of the sacred core contradicts the claim to honour it. The severity surprises only if speech is treated as harmless decoration. Here speech functions as evidence of allegiance, and contempt toward revelation breaks the claim from within.

phrases.translation: If We pardon a group of you, We will punish others for their wickedness
phrases.explanation: Pardon for a group and punishment for others preserve individual difference inside a shared incident. Early reports mention at least one participant who repented sincerely and changed course. Wickedness in the punished group points to persistence rather than a single careless sentence. The verse therefore combines a closed excuse with an open door for genuine turning.

phrases.translation: The hypocrites, both men and women, are all alike: they encourage what is evil,
phrases.explanation: Hypocrite men and women are described as one pattern repeated across persons. Encouraging evil means their influence moves outward, normalising disobedience and making wrongdoing socially easier. This shared programme replaces the mutual support found among believers later in the chapter. Alikeness is moral rather than biological, because the same inward refusal produces the same public direction.

phrases.translation: forbid what is good, and withhold ˹what is in˺ their hands.
phrases.explanation: Forbidding good and withholding hands complete the reversal. They discourage prayer, charity, courage, and sacrifice while keeping wealth tightly closed. A clenched hand pictures miserliness without needing a long description. Their community life is therefore destructive in advice and useless in generosity, since both words and money are turned away from the purposes Allah loves.

phrases.translation: They neglected Allah, so He neglected them. Surely the hypocrites are the rebellious
phrases.explanation: Neglecting Allah leads to being neglected by Him, a fitting return in which those who forget the covenant lose care and favour. The language does not mean divine forgetfulness in a human sense. It means abandonment to the consequence of chosen distance. Rebellious gathers the portrait into one word, since every mark flows from refusing rightful authority.

phrases.translation: Allah has promised the hypocrites, both men and women, and the disbelievers an everlasting stay in the Fire of Hell—it is sufficient for them.
phrases.explanation: The promise to hypocrites and disbelievers is an everlasting stay in the Fire, using promise language with grim finality. It is sufficient for them means the punishment fully answers the life chosen, leaving no need for an added penalty to make the return complete. Men and women are named again so the warning covers the whole pattern without exception.

phrases.translation: Allah has condemned them, and they will suffer a never-ending punishment
phrases.explanation: Condemnation from Allah means distance from mercy, joined here with punishment that does not end.
